summary.text: A 74-year-old right-handed, unemployed man who was a current smoker with a medical history significant only for hypertension presented after a fall with comminuted fractures of the middle phalangeal bases of the right middle and ring fingers. Initial radiographs showed comminuted depressed fractures at the base of the middle phalanges of both digits, and CT showed articular surface comminution and depression, a dorsal fracture at the central slip insertion and a longitudinal fracture line extending into the diaphysis.

Traction-type external fixation was considered impractical because of multi-digit involvement, so open reduction and internal fixation with a locking plate was planned. Surgery under brachial plexus block anesthesia on day 3 after injury used a dorsal midline incision, anatomic reduction, diaphyseal soft stainless steel wires, granular artificial bone and a Y-shaped plate with cortical and locking screws, with a central slip wire tied to the plate. The same technique was applied to the ring finger; operative time was 3.5 h with minimal blood loss.

Gentle active ROM exercises began on the first postoperative day using a relative motion extension protocol, with the injured fingers immobilized in extension during rest for the first 4 weeks. CT at 3 months postoperatively showed good bone union with well stabilized fragments, good concentric alignment and a slight residual step-off in the ring finger.

At the 12-month postoperative final follow-up range of motion was favorable, and radiographs at 12 months showed no progression of PIP joint degenerative changes. Without a stated time, grip strength was 24 kg (89 % of the contralateral side), with a mild middle finger swan-neck deformity, no pain, no implant discomfort, mild DIP joint osteoarthritic changes and unrestricted activities of daily living.

ambiguities.issue: The recommendation about implant removal follows the sentence on thin dorsal finger soft tissue and may be a general recommendation rather than a plan for this patient.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not infer that implant removal was planned, requested or performed for this patient.

ambiguities.issue: The ring finger fracture is called comminuted depressed on radiographs (both digits) and incomplete at the dorsal base of the middle phalanx in the operative text; the two statements may describe different parts of the fracture rather than conflict.

ambiguities.issue: The final follow-up paragraph opens with the 12-month postoperative follow-up for range of motion, but grip strength, the swan-neck deformity, absence of pain, absence of implant discomfort, the DIP joint osteoarthritic change and activities of daily living are stated in later sentences without their own time; the Fig. 6 caption time covers only its range-of-motion statement.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not assign the 12-month time to these findings.

caption_evidence.quote:
Fig. 3
Intraoperative schema and photographs. A: Dotted line indicating the extensor hood incision. B: Elevation and proximal reflection of the articular fragment at the base of the middle phalanx, preserving continuity with the central slip.C, D: Longitudinal traction was applied to the affected finger, and the articular surface was anatomically reduced under direct visualization. Two 0.32 mm stainless steel wires (arrow) were inserted into the diaphysis to gather the comminuted fragments.E: Bone voids following reduction were filled with granular artificial bone to support the subchondral bone. A 0.32 mm cerclage wire (arrowhead) was passed through the central slip attachment site of the reflected articular fragment.F, G: The dorsal articular fragment of the middle phalanx was reduced, and the diaphyseal wires were tightened to bundle the bone fragments. H, I: A plate was positioned just proximal to the articular surface along the path of the wires, and locking screws were inserted under fluoroscopic guidance to provide subchondral support. J, K: Finally, the cerclage wire passed through the central slip was tied to the plate to reinforce fixation of the dorsal articular fragment.
Fig. 3
